name: Bianca Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the stockwoman on my uncle Paolo's beef farm, about a hundred and fifty suckler cows, mostly Hereford crosses, and eighty hectares we cut for hay. In winter it's feeding, bedding and checking for anything off, which takes until about two. Then it's fixing whatever's broken, usually a gate or the bale handler. In summer it's all about the hay and the weather.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy calving, believe it or not, even at three in the morning. And there's nothing like a barn full of good hay in September. The hard bit is the weather, and machines breaking at the worst moment. My boyfriend Luca's a mechanic, which is handy, but he's not always free when the baler dies.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. I've never seen the need. I do the herd records on the computer because I have to, and that's as far as it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So, basically nothing. That sounds about right to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: wait and see, most new things are oversold. People get excited, the salesman turns up, and two years later it's in a shed with a sheet over it. I wouldn't post about it, I don't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be relieved, but I'd also think I was right not to bother learning any of it. The cattle don't care about computers. My worry would still be the usual ones, beef prices, feed costs and the price of diesel for the tractors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going exactly as I am. Keep putting a bit by each month, like I have since I was nineteen. I might finally get the new silage clamp sorted with Paolo, which has nothing to do with AI at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal. It's a normal year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said most new things end up in a shed with a sheet over them. Any examples?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paolo bought a cattle weighing system with a camera about four years ago. It worked for one winter, then the software needed paying for every year, so it's in the back of the shed. We went back to the old scales and they've never once needed an update.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you put the savings towards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly nothing yet, it just sits there, plus my gran left me a six-acre field near the village. It's rented out for grazing. One day it'll be a house or it'll be the start of my own herd, I haven't decided.

S0.say: She'd say what she always says: wait and see, because most new things are oversold and end up in a shed under a sheet. She wouldn't post about it.
S0.think: She'd feel relieved and proved right not to learn any of it. Her real worries would stay the usual ones: beef prices, feed and diesel.
S0.do: Keeps working as before, keeps saving a set amount each month as she has since nineteen, and plans a new silage clamp with her uncle.
S0.feel: Calm, as in any normal year.
S0.quote: We went back to the old scales and they've never once needed an update.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca's scepticism is built on real experience, the camera weighing system now in the back of the shed. Her centre outlook shows as practical doubt rather than anger at anyone. She has a quiet asset, a field from her grandmother, and hasn't decided what to do with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That's more believable than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for the arable lads and the big dairy units, not small beef. Cattle on hill pasture, hay off old meadows, that's not where the robots go first. I'd say it calmly, though, I'm not one for panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit worried, because Paolo's sixty and his son wants nothing to do with the farm. If the land agent tells him a contractor with robot balers can do the hay for half the price, I'm one person he doesn't need in the summer. I'd still have the cattle work, but it'd be less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the neighbours did, that's honestly my first move. I'd keep saving and maybe stop spending on holidays for a year to be safe. If Paolo started talking about contractors, I'd have a proper talk with him about me taking over some of the herd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just watching the sky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't learning the robot balers yourself keep you in the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I'm not a computer person, and I'd be no better than the contractor's lad. Where I'm useful is knowing which cow's about to calve before she knows it. That doesn't go on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Paolo about taking over the herd?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'll pay a fair rent and do it properly. He's always said I'm the only one who loves the cattle. I'd remind him of that, gently.

S1.say: She'd calmly say the change is for big arable and dairy farms, not small beef on hill pasture. Robots won't come for old hay meadows first.
S1.think: Privately she worries her uncle, sixty and without a successor, would hire a contractor with robot balers for half the cost. She'd keep the cattle work but lose her summer hay work.
S1.do: Waits to see what the neighbours do, keeps saving and skips a holiday for a year. If her uncle talks about contractors, proposes taking over part of the herd on a fair rent.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like someone watching the sky for rain.
S1.quote: Where I'm useful is knowing which cow's about to calve before she knows it. That doesn't go on a screen.
S1.fieldNote: Bianca's say and think diverge: publicly calm, privately aware of a real gap in summer work. She defends her value as stock sense, not technology. Her plan is to move closer to owning, not to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then it doesn't matter what I think, it's happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody knows how this will go, and people should keep their heads. I wouldn't join any marches, that's not me. I'd say the government needs to look after people who lose work, but it shouldn't throw money around either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be frightened. If a robot can calve a cow and spot pneumonia in a calf, then my one skill is gone. And I've never even used the chatbot, so I'd be starting from further back than everybody else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop spending and keep the cash close. I'd ask Paolo to sell or rent me part of the herd before anyone else makes him an offer. I'd probably build a little house on gran's field, because a roof you own is worth more than money in a bank if everything goes strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach goes tight just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having just two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can't even wait and see, which is my whole method. By the time I've seen, it's done. That's what scares me most, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI tools now, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose I'd have to try, wouldn't I? Luca would set it up on my phone. I'd probably use it once, get annoyed and put the phone in the glovebox.

S2.say: She'd tell people to keep their heads, saying nobody knows how it will go. She'd support help for those who lose work but warn against throwing money around, and wouldn't march.
S2.think: Privately she'd be frightened: if a robot can calve a cow and spot pneumonia, her one skill is gone, and she'd be starting from further back than others because she has never used AI.
S2.do: Stops spending and keeps cash close, asks her uncle to sell or rent her part of the herd before anyone else offers, and builds a small house on her grandmother's field.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with a tight stomach at the thought of it.
S2.quote: It means I can't even wait and see, which is my whole method. By the time I've seen, it's done.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture breaks Bianca's main strategy, waiting to see, and she names that herself. Under pressure she turns to tangible things: cattle, a field, a roof she owns. She doubts she'd stick with AI even if she tried it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better. I can at least watch someone else go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious and people should plan, but calmly. I'd probably say it at the young farmers' club, keep money aside, don't buy big machines on credit right now. That's the sort of thing I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd spend the first two years hoping it wouldn't really happen, like the hype one. Then I'd see robots at the cattle market or on the dairy farm down the road, and I'd panic a bit late. I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard and start the house on gran's field in year one or two. I'd rent part of Paolo's herd so I'm an owner, not just staff. And I'd let Luca drag me to a course on the new machines, probably year three, after I'd seen them work properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like knowing the vet's coming with bad news, just not this week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd panic a bit late. What would you want to do early instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get my name on the land and the cattle. That's the bit that has to happen early, because once everyone's selling, the prices go strange. The learning can wait, the paperwork can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think would be responsible if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody and everybody. The companies would say they just made a product, the government would say nobody saw it coming. I don't really blame any one of them, which probably sounds odd.

S3.say: She'd tell the young farmers' club it's serious but to plan calmly: keep money aside and don't buy big machines on credit right now.
S3.think: She expects to spend two years hoping it won't happen, then panic slightly late once she sees robots at the cattle market or on the dairy farm nearby.
S3.do: Saves hard and starts building a house on her grandmother's field within two years, rents part of her uncle's herd so she becomes an owner, and takes a course on the new machines in about year three once she's seen them work.
S3.feel: Anxious, like waiting for the vet with bad news that isn't due yet.
S3.quote: Get my name on the land and the cattle. That's the bit that has to happen early
S3.fieldNote: With five years Bianca separates what must happen early (ownership) from what can wait (learning). Her blame is spread thin, which fits her centre outlook. She predicts her own slow reaction with real self-knowledge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough that I'd honestly stop thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so let's not get carried away. Keep farming, keep an eye on it. I'd say that at the market and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is when I'd really have to take over from Paolo anyway. So the robots would land right when I'm in charge of the herd and the hay. That's either good timing or the worst timing, I can't tell which.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take over the herd properly over the first few years, on a long lease. I'd build the house on gran's field. I'd try a bit of the new kit once the neighbours had it working, probably around year five, and I'd keep saving the way I always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a bit of unease at the back. It's far off enough to feel like the weather forecast for next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop thinking about it. Is that a good or bad thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad, probably. But it's how I'd be. Luca would be the one reminding me every Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the cattle side to look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Smaller herd, better cattle, sold direct to people who care where their beef comes from. If robots do the hay, fine, as long as I'm the one standing in the field deciding when to cut.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty of time, so people shouldn't get carried away: keep farming and keep an eye on it.
S4.think: Privately she notes that ten years is roughly when she'd take over from her uncle anyway, so the robots would arrive just as she's in charge, which is either very good or very bad timing.
S4.do: Takes over the herd on a long lease over the first few years, builds the house on her grandmother's field, keeps saving, and tries the new machines around year five once neighbours have them working.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a little unease, like a forecast for next month.
S4.quote: If robots do the hay, fine, as long as I'm the one standing in the field deciding when to cut.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Bianca go back to her preferred pace, and she admits she'd stop thinking about it. Her ideal future keeps the decisions human even if the work isn't. Her partner Luca again appears as the person who nudges her on technology.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Waiting and seeing is how I do everything, and it wouldn't work. What would help is plain information, from people who farm, about what actually works, not salesmen. And some way for young people to get onto land before the big buyers sweep it up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the animals. Nobody asked who'll notice when a cow's not right. I'd want that to stay someone's job, whatever else happens.

headlineQuote: It means I can't even wait and see, which is my whole method. By the time I've seen, it's done.
portrait: Bianca Costa is a 27-year-old stockwoman on her uncle's beef and hay farm who has never used an AI tool and doesn't plan to. Her method for everything is to wait and see, backed by real stories of gadgets that ended up in the shed. Pragmatic and in the middle politically, she spreads blame thinly and dislikes both panic and waste. Under pressure she reaches for solid things: cattle, her grandmother's field, a house she owns. The two-year picture frightens her most because it takes away the time she needs to watch others go first.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her habit of waiting to see would no longer work.
whatWouldHelp: Plain, honest information from working farmers about what works, and a way for young people to get onto land before big buyers take it.
